definition: Philanthropy means organized generosity toward humanity — giving money, time, or effort on a large scale to improve other people's lives.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word philanthropy. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know philanthropy should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The aquarium owes its new research wing to local philanthropy: three families quietly covered what years of ticket sales never could.
Kindness is the smallest coin of the three: one door held, one gentle word — far short of philanthropy, which builds the hospital the gentle word is spoken in.
Generosity is broader than kindness but still stops short of philanthropy: a generous person picks up the check, while a philanthropist endows the culinary school.

Charity means help given directly to those in need — a meal, a coat, a donation; philanthropy works at longer range, funding libraries, cures, and scholarships meant to fix causes rather than symptoms.
Benevolence means the disposition to wish others well; benevolence can stay a feeling, while philanthropy is benevolence with a budget — the wish turned into funded action.
Generosity means openhandedness of any kind, to anyone — picking up a check, forgiving a debt; philanthropy aims that openhandedness at the public good, usually through causes and institutions.

Philanthropy means organized generosity toward humanity — giving money, time, or effort on a large scale to improve other people's lives.
Late in life, the steel magnate turned to philanthropy with the same ferocity he had brought to business, spending his fortune down on 2,500 public libraries and declaring it a disgrace to die rich.
The scale and the aim are what make this philanthropy rather than a good deed: organized wealth pointed at the public's long-term good — literacy for strangers he would never meet.
Greek phil- ('loving') plus anthropos ('human being') says it plainly: love of humankind, with a checkbook.

Philanthropy is the boardroom-and-broadsheet word for giving: it implies scale, organization, and a public aim, and it often names the whole sector — 'a career in philanthropy.' For one warm act, kindness or generosity fits better; for direct relief of need, charity.
The person is a philanthropist; the adjective (which you may meet on test day) is philanthropic.

When the river district flooded in 1998, the response came in two waves.
The first was charity: neighbors hauling furniture upstairs, church halls full of cots and soup.
The second wave took longer and made fewer photographs.
An anonymous donor spent eleven years buying up the floodplain, then gave it to the county as a wetland — engineered to absorb the next flood before it reached a single porch.
Reporters called the gift philanthropy of the least sentimental kind: no plaque, no gala, just a budget aimed at the cause of the misery rather than its symptoms.
The cots have long been folded away; the wetland is still working every time it rains.
